original_value: AbstractCompelling research has recently shown that cancer is so heterogeneous that single research centres cannot produce enough data to fit prognostic and predictive models of sufficient accuracy. Data sharing in precision oncology is therefore of utmost importance. The Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable (FAIR) Data Principles have been developed to define good practices in data sharing. Motivated by the ambition of applying the FAIR Data Principles to our own clinical precision oncology implementations and research, we have performed a systematic literature review of potentially relevant initiatives. For clinical data, we suggest using the Genomic Data Commons model as a reference as it provides a field-tested and well-documented solution. Regarding classification of diagnosis, morphology and topography and drugs, we chose to follow the World Health Organization standards, i.e. ICD10, ICD-O-3 and Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classifications, respectively. For the bioinformatics pipeline, the Genome Analysis ToolKit Best Practices using Docker containers offer a coherent solution and have therefore been selected. Regarding the naming of variants, we follow the Human Genome Variation Society's standard. For the IT infrastructure, we have built a centralized solution to participate in data sharing through federated solutions such as the Beacon Networks.

result.paraphrase: Recent research shows that cancer is highly heterogeneous, making it impossible for a single research centre to generate enough data to build prognostic and predictive models with adequate accuracy. Data sharing in precision oncology is therefore essential. The FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable) Data Principles were created to set out best practices for sharing data. Driven by our aim to apply these principles to our own clinical precision oncology implementations and research, we conducted a systematic literature review of potentially relevant initiatives. For clinical data, we recommend the Genomic Data Commons model as a reference because it is a well-documented, field-tested solution. For diagnosis, morphology, topography and drugs, we chose the World Health Organization standards: ICD10, ICD-O-3 and Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classifications, respectively. For the bioinformatics pipeline, we selected the Genome Analysis ToolKit Best Practices using Docker containers, as they provide a coherent solution. For variant naming, we follow the Human Genome Variation Society standard. For IT infrastructure, we have developed a centralized solution to enable participation in data sharing through federated systems such as the Beacon Networks.
